item.text: {"question_id":"5B.9","answer":"In 2023, the Sisi government pursued several responses to inflation, foreign-exchange, food-security, and debt pressures. These included a $3 billion IMF program, expanded Takaful and Karama coverage, emergency food-security measures that supported uninterrupted bread subsidies, September cost-of-living, wage, tax, and transfer increases, and directed debt-relief measures for small farmers (BATCH-0006-E006; BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0022-E005; BATCH-0022-E006). The emergency food-security intervention was externally financed and operationally described, but the presidentially announced transfers and debt relief lack supplied evidence of execution, funding, uptake, or purchasing-power effects. Targeting and correction were materially inadequate: reported transfers covered about one-third of families living in or near poverty and were eroded by currency devaluation and inflation; IMF reviews due in March and June were postponed to year-end after transparency criteria were not met; and electricity cutbacks appeared longer in rural and impoverished areas, disrupting work, health care, and water access (BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0009-R07-E010; BATCH-0009-R07-E011). Inflation nevertheless reached 39.7 percent in August, and debt vulnerability remained high, although external shocks—including the pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, global price increases, high interest rates, capital outflows, and tight global financial conditions—substantially qualify attribution for the deterioration (BATCH-0007-E020; BATCH-0003-E013; BATCH-0020-E010; BATCH-0019-E010). Overall, the evidence supports active crisis-response efforts and some externally supported implementation, but not a finding of consistently timely, transparently targeted, monitored, or corrected
